name: Gareth Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to any company, union, party or government. It's all confidential, so you can tell me your public line and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a share farmer at Oakes Farm. That means the landowner, Mrs Oakes, provides the land and buildings, I provide the labour, the pigs and half the machinery, and we split what the crops make. I've got 60 outdoor sows, and we grow barley and oilseed rape on about 90 hectares. Morning's feeding the pigs and checking the arcs, which are the tin huts they live in, then field work or fixing fences.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everywhere I can fit it. I've got a camera that weighs pigs as they walk past the feeder, a drone that maps the barley for weeds, and I ask an AI assistant about grain prices every morning. I'm paying off a GPS tractor over five years. People call me the gadget lad, and I don't mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit disappointing, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the tools are still useful even if they're not magic. The weighing camera saves me two hours a week, and that's real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. My worry was always the pig price, which goes in cycles, and I've got about three months of savings to ride out a bad spell. AI being hype doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I've got and add a few more, like the field sensor kits from the merchant. I'd pay the tractor down on schedule. Business as usual, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit let down, because I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a bad pig price year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lose money on every pig for about six months. I've done it once, in 2024. I'd cut the sow numbers to 50 and live on beans for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your agreement with Mrs Oakes that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It renews every five years, next in 2029. Mrs Oakes is 70 and fair, but her son lives in London and sees the farm as a bank account.

I'd point out the **weighing camera** saves me two hours a week.
think: I'm fine; my real risk is the **pig price cycle**.
About **three months** of savings can ride out a bad spell.

Pay down the **GPS tractor** on schedule.
Keep the 60 sows and crops as **business as usual**.
feel: **Calm**, a bit **let down** because he likes new things.

steps.text: Buy field sensor kits from the merchant this year
Keep using the pig weighing camera and drone maps
Keep 60 sows and pay the tractor on schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That's the one I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms that adopt early will do well, and the ones that wait will struggle. I'd say it on the farmers' forum online, probably too loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this is good for me. My job's mostly hands-on and the paperwork, buying and booking would get easier. I'd be ahead of most neighbours, and I could sell that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a side business doing drone weed maps for neighbouring farms, about £8 a hectare. I'd put £4,000 into a robot pig feeder trial by 2028. And I'd let AI run my grain selling, with me checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A bit nervous about spending money ahead of the proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older farmers round here who won't use a smartphone. Mr Bryce at Low Farm still does his grain sales by phone with the merchant. Mr Bryce would be getting a worse price every year and not know why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your enthusiasm cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's fair. I've bought gadgets that didn't work, like a pig thermometer that broke in the rain. So I'd try things small first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different animal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so get on board. I'd be the one at the pub saying buy the robots before they buy you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd admit. In 2028 the AI does all my planning and marketing, which is fine. But my agreement with Mrs Oakes renews in 2029, and once robots arrive in 2031, her son could rent the land to a company with a fleet of robots and skip me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop buying new kit and pay off the tractor early, so I'm debt-free by 2029. I'd grow the drone mapping into a proper business, so I've got income that isn't tied to Mrs Oakes's land. And I'd try to sign a ten-year agreement with Mrs Oakes before 2028, with robots in my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited about the tech, anxious about the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's everything. The thinking bits change in 2028, which I'm ready for. The three years after are my chance to show Mrs Oakes I'm the one who runs her robots, not the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mrs Oakes's son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mrs Oakes's son that I can run his land with robots cheaper than any company, because I know every wet corner of the farm. Whether he listens is another thing.

I'd tell people at the pub to **buy the robots** before they buy you.
think: My **land agreement** renews in 2029, just before robots arrive.

S2.quote: I'd tell Mrs Oakes's son that I can run his land with robots cheaper than any company, because I know every wet corner of the farm.
fieldNote: His tech skills don't remove his **land tenure** risk.

He shifts from investing to **paying off debt**.

steps.text: Pay off the GPS tractor early to be debt-free by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to get positioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now. I'd be telling every young farmer I know to learn the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years fits me well. The agreement renews in 2029, before AGI in 2031. I could sign a longer deal with Mrs Oakes, build up the robots, and by 2034 be running the whole farm with machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign a ten-year agreement in 2029 with a robot plan built in. I'd invest about £15,000 in robot kit between 2030 and 2033. I'd keep using AI tools daily and stay ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would £15,000 come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings, the drone mapping income and a bank loan for the rest. I'd only borrow once the agreement's signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be uneasy about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Oakes's health, really. If something happened to Mrs Oakes, the son would decide. Everything I build here would still be on somebody else's land.

fieldNote: Timing works for him: the **renewal lands first**.

steps.text: Install robot feeders and weeders across Oakes Farm by 2033

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's the dream timeline for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, not a threat, if you plan. I'd be the one telling everyone to get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the best one for me. I'd be 37 when AGI comes and 40 when robots arrive, with time to save, maybe even buy a bit of land. I think I'd come out ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to buy 20 hectares of my own by 2032, with a mortgage. I'd grow the robot side of the business slowly. And I'd keep the pigs, because I like them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty optimistic, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything still on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I'll be lonely. Running a farm with robots is a quiet life, and I like people more than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably join the young farmers' club again, or run the drone business so I'm on other people's farms. I'd make sure I've got reasons to talk to humans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of the land. The tech doesn't scare me, but my agreement does. What would help is longer, safer agreements for share farmers and tenants, so young people can invest without losing it all.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked who's ready. I think young farmers are more ready for robots than people assume. What young farmers aren't ready for is not owning the ground we stand on.

headlineQuote: What young farmers aren't ready for is not owning the ground we stand on.
portrait: Gareth is a 27-year-old **share farmer** with 60 outdoor sows on Oakes Farm.
He uses **AI daily** and sees robots mostly as an opportunity.
His real exposure is **land tenure**, since the agreement renews in 2029.
He stays **calm** in mild pictures and becomes **anxious** at AGI by 2028.
With ten years, he plans to **buy land**, but worries about loneliness.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his land agreement could go to a robot company.
whatWouldHelp: **Longer, safer agreements** for share farmers and tenants, so they can invest.
